item.title: The Making of Oxygene
item.description:
Access All Areas / By Mark Gidley

The Making of Oxygene

The full story of the ground-breaking Oxygene album and how it has been re-imagined for Dolby Atmos

01/Feature

Oxygene - The History

In late 1976, an album was released which re-wrote the rulebook of synthesizers and electronic music and captured the hearts and imagination of the entire world. Composed by the then unknown 28-year-old French artist Jean-Michel Jarre, the album Oxygène broke out of France to become a top 10 album in seven different countries, spending a remarkable 24 weeks in the UK album charts and selling now close to 20 million copies worldwide.

Uniquely, the album consisted of just six tracks, numbered Oxygène Parts 1 through 6, and was entirely instrumental with no acoustic instruments whatsoever, which was unheard of in 1976.

Jean Michel Jarre tells the story of the making of his ground-breaking album in his own words.

"Around 1969, I felt that the world of classical music, the world of rock and other forms of music were a bit narrow and living in their own worlds. I had the feeling it was the right time to explore other fields to perhaps see if a combination of different styles were possible.

“The main difference with electronic music is that you create music in terms of sound, not just notes. It’s something else entirely. When I was a teenager, I always liked processing my guitar or organ or whatever, playing the tape backwards and changing the speed. Then the drummer in my band said, ‘You should meet with these crazy guys at Groupe De Recherches Musicales [GRM] in Paris who are working in French public radio. They’re doing the same kinds of things as you, and they have labs.’

“When I first went there, I was immediately seduced by what they were doing. Electronic music owes a lot to public radio stations - the BBC Radiophonic Workshop, the German lab where Stockhausen was working and, of course, the one in Paris.

"Pierre Schaeffer was one of the most brilliant guys of the century in terms of what he brought to the music world. He created the notion of Musique concrète and influenced me a lot in this direction. Saying that, I felt that contemporary music had got a very elitist attitude - a bit too intellectual vis-à-vis the music and it created barriers between the audience and yourself. I wanted to be much more open to the audience.

"I stayed with Pierre Schaeffer [and Pierre Henry] for three years and I also went to Cologne to work with Stockhausen. He was totally crazy, but a real genius. He considered himself to be made of sound, biologically, so he had a kind of surrealistic approach. Crazy, but realistic at the same time. It was very interesting.

"When I left GRM and through to 1976, I did production work for some rock artists, earning enough to set up a studio in my kitchen. I didn’t have much equipment, though, just a few guitar pedals and my first synthesizer, the VCS3, which looked like a telephone exchange. I realised that using a Revox tape machine to delay the sound that came out of one loudspeaker created a huge sense of space.

“The British-made VCS3 from EMS [Electronic Music Studios, based in London] was created by a genius called Peter Zinovieff. It was a kind of poor European version of the Moog. In those days Europe was not as rich as the States, so the sound was drier. In a sense, it was a kind of punk synthesizer - there was something very harsh and rough about it. I loved it; I still take one on stage with me today.

“At the time, I was obsessed with this idea of creating a bridge between experimentation and pop melody. I liked this kind of challenge, playing around with sound design and integrating melodies. Oxygène was a new start for music with analogue synthesizers"

The album was recorded on a Scully recorder with just eight tracks, and all through a home-made mixer. On top of the VCS3, Jarre had managed to add some other classic equipment including EMS Synthi AKS and ARP 2600 synths, an Eminent String Ensemble, an RMI Harmonic Synthesizer, and Farfisa organ, while an RMI Keyboard Computer was used for some sequencing.

Jarre continues, “I really did it in a kind of home way using what, I think, was one of the first home studios. I had just three or four synthesizers and was using a Scully eight–track and a mixture of Ampex 256 and 3M tape. The whole album was done on just one eight–track and you can hear that in the piece — it’s quite minimalist and I think that contributes to its timelessness.

“Nothing is repeated the same way. Each sound, even if appears to be the same, has a slightly different attack and release, and, as the sequences are being made by hand, by definition they are not the same. Even the sounds of the drum machines were filtered in a very subtle way to give life inside the patterns.

”Michel Geiss was a maintenance technician, at a famous French record company at that time called Barclay and I met him because he was very interested in electronic instruments. He visited my home and we started to experiment. He was teaching me to use the first semi-modular synths I could put my hands on. And then step by step we worked together, Michel mainly as a kind of sound engineer for me.

“For Oxygene, he was working at his record company as a maintenance guy during the day, and he was coming to work with me at night. In those days I probably had the first home studio in France, when the serious music was done in serious recording studios with a window where God was the sound engineer behind the window, and we were just on the other side as musicians. For electronic music you need to match the mixing area with the main studio to record your own sounds.

“So, I had this home studio in a kitchen in the flat I had in Paris, and Michel joined me, using one of the first eight-track tape recorders to record my music. I only had two tapes. So, I had no choice if I was not happy with something to erase what I'd done the previous day, and this is the reason why I have no archive of material from Oxygène. It's such a shame.

“And that is also the reason why if you take the master tape of Oxygène, it is made up of two different tapes. Right in the middle of part one of Oxygène, I had one piece I really liked, where suddenly in the first part you have this kind of brassy, quite epic brassy moment. This is coming from another tape that I recorded another time.

“I thought to myself that it's really matching very well. So, I did a very strong edit, quite dramatic edit, by cutting the two tapes together, even the colours are different. One is pink, one is black. It's totally crazy. And whilst you can't hear the edit, it's quite challenging to cut an eight-track tape like this.

“With so little to work with, I had to be creative. My old Mellotron only had a few working keys, but I still managed to write Oxygene Part II on it. My primitive drum machine - a Korg Mini Pops was the sort of thing people played in pubs, but by using Sellotape I could make it play two preset rhythms at the same time, creating cool beats. Oxygène Part IV, which became iconic, was a mixture of [presets] Slow Rock and Rock, while Part VI combined Rumba and Bossa Nova.

“But when I finished the album, because Oxygène consisted of entirely instrumental music, none of the record companies thought it would work. The only people who took the risk were a small French company called Dreyfus Music. Even after it had become a hit in France, people said it couldn't possibly be a success anywhere else. Then eventually, after it got to the top of the charts in Britain and all over Europe, the critics explained that it was successful because of its originality and because of its use of melody. It's easy to be wise after the event!

“I made the first album back in the days of vinyl, when we were always thinking about sides one and two. The other characteristic of Oxygène is that it has sunny melodies but it’s also quite dark, like the cover artwork.”

Studio engineer and would-be long-time collaborator Michel Geiss, has fond memories of his first encounter with Jean Michel Jarre, recalling, "Oxygene marked the beginning of my collaboration with Jean-Michel. At the time, I was working during the day at a large studio complex in Paris called Studios Barclay. I was employed there as a technician. The recording studios were located on the upper floors, while I worked in the workshop downstairs. My body was downstairs, but my mind was upstairs! I felt strongly attracted to the world of music engineering, although I wasn't particularly interested in the equipment I had been assigned to work with.

"In fact, I found the right balance when I began working with Jean-Michel at his own studio around the same time. Every day, once my working day at Barclay had finished, I would join Jean-Michel in his studio, at his request, to work on his album. We would continue until I had to catch the last train home. I remember him calling me every afternoon to ask if I could come over.

"This was my first real opportunity to work in a studio as a sound and music collaborator, and I thoroughly enjoyed it. Jean-Michel would also occasionally ask for my musical opinion on various matters. I programmed some specific sounds on the ARP 2600, including the main theme sound in Oxygene IV and the sound of the waves in Part VI.

"It was a close working relationship, and I felt that I had finally found my rightful place. It suited me much better than simply being an electronics specialist, which was my background before I met him.

"My main role during the recording of Oxygene was to record Jean-Michel while he played his instruments, as he needed someone to handle the recording process.

"At the time, he was also keen to expand his relatively limited collection of instruments in order to explore new sounds. I suggested that we take a look at the RMI keyboards, which were sold in France by Piano Center in Montreuil. Jean-Michel immediately agreed, saying, 'OK, let's go!'

"When we arrived at the music shop, Jean-Michel discovered the two instruments I had suggested: the RMI Harmonic Synthesizer and the RMI Keyboard Computer. The latter used punched cardboard cards to store its sound information. The Harmonic Synthesizer had a truly distinctive sound and featured an arpeggiator. It would later prove to be a key instrument on the album, particularly on Oxygene IV."

The album’s iconic artwork came about when Jarre was visiting Marquet Gallery in Paris and a piece caught his eye that he was instantly drawn to. A painting of a skull hidden within the Earth. The painting was created by young artist Michel Granger, titled Oxygène. By chance, Granger happened to be in the gallery at the same time and the pair spoke and Jean-Michel bought the painting to use as the album cover and adopted its title.

Michel Granger recalls, “I was having my first major show in Paris. On display was a 30x40cm watercolour called Oxygène and Jean-Michel bought it, telling me he’d love to use it as an album cover. Oxygène was part of a series about the damage being done to our planet. It was quite a violent image for a record sleeve.

“The only change I made was to the background, making it square to fit the album shape. Jean-Michel and I chose the typography and that was that. We were both similar ages and he was very passionate about music and painting. We would have long conversations in the evenings, always at the same pizzeria, then he went home to compose all night.”

Jean Michel Jarre commented on the artwork,"What I like about this picture is that it isn’t necessarily pessimistic. It rather poses the question: where are we going?”

With its iconic title and cover set, and after the album was mixed at Studio Gang by Jean-Pierre Janiaud, an accomplished engineer, Jarre took the album to Francis Dreyfus, owner of the Disques Motors record label, who he had worked for during his songwriting days with Christophe. Dreyfus loved the album and was convinced it could be a success.

Dreyfus pressed 50,000 copies on his own label to sell in France and released the album in December 1976. Uniquely and a brainwave of Dreyfus and Jarre, they offered the album to nationwide hi-fi shops, given the album's innovative use of stereo. The idea being that high-end hi-fi buyers would buy a copy of the album to go with their hardware purchase. By April 1977, sales in France had reached 70,000 copies despite very little promotion. Legend has it that some people returned the LP believing the iconic white noise was a manufacturing defect.

Finding an international label to distribute was harder. Initially no record company was interested in the album, citing no singer, no guitars, no drummer, no proper track titles, no obvious singles, and to round it off, it was French.

Everything changed when Fred Haayen, the new head of Polydor Records in London discovered the record in a French record store and signed it to the label. He was instrumental in persuading BBC Radio 1 to play the album in full the week of release. The only other album to ever receive such an honour was Pink Floyd's Dark Side of the Moon.

The album was mostly slated by the UK's mainstream music press, with the NME calling it “another interminable sonic cruise and infuriatingly derivative.” but the public loved the album and on August 23rd 1977, Oxygène entered the UK album charts at number 19, climbing and remaining in the top 10 for the next 11 weeks. After moving to the United States to lead Polydor USA, Haayen also spearheaded the launch of the album in the US, to achieve official platinum status.

We’ll let Jarre conclude the story, “It’s now sold something like 18 million copies and, no matter what I do, I am defined by Oxygène. But that’s OK. It’s funny. At first, the album was played in hi-fi shops as an example of 'state-of-the-art sound'. I didn’t tell them I made it in my kitchen.

“When you’ve been lucky enough to have some kind of success with your first project, it will always be part of your DNA, no matter what you do afterwards. It’s like the first movie for Tarantino or Kubrick. For me, it’s the same with Oxygène. I love many other things that I’ve done and I’m very proud of them all, but Oxygène is something unique.”

When you’ve been lucky enough to have some kind of success with your first project, it will always be part of your DNA, no matter what you do afterwards. I love many other things that I’ve done and I’m very proud of them all, but Oxygène is something unique.

02/Feature

Oxygene 50th Anniversary

Jean-Michel Jarre will release a 50th anniversary edition of his breakthrough album, Oxygene, on November 20 2026.

Jarre originally released the album in France in 1976, ahead of its international release in 1977, Oxygene helped bring electronic music to a global audience and established Jarre as one of the figureheads of the genre.

At the heart of the anniversary edition is a new 2026 remaster of the original stereo mix, created from the original tapes to restore the full dynamics and character of the recording.

“When I created Oxygene, I was working directly with analogue instruments and tape, and the sound had a particular depth, movement and life of its own," he recalls. "For this anniversary edition, we returned to the original tapes with the aim of preserving that character rather than changing it”.

The release includes a 180g black-vinyl edition, half-speed mastered and cut by Miles Showell at Abbey Road Studios; CD; limited-edition coloured eco-vinyl; digital editions; and a deluxe Blu-ray mediabook featuring Oxygene in Dolby Atmos for the first time, alongside a new 5.1 mix, the 2026 stereo remaster and selected archival material.

03/Feature

Oxygene - Dolby Atmos release

Oxygene has been mixed in Dolby Atmos and 5.1 Surround by David Kosten, Steven Wilson and Jean-Michel Jarre, from the original multi-tracks, with sessions in Paris and London to perfect these immersive mixes.

Speaking about the process, Jean Michel Jarre observed, "It was quite challenging for David because I originally recorded Oxygene on eight tracks, and because you have a lot of things going on on the same track, you have lots of different elements. You can go from a bass to a sound effect to some pads. And David had to separate all this coming from the same original track and after that then the next challenge was to put the different audio objects into space."

David Kosten reflected, "Once the hard work of recreating the original mixes is done, I start to think about how to present the music in three dimensions. Any sound can be placed anywhere so there's a lot of choices to make across an entire album! With Atmos we have speakers in front, to the side, behind and above the listener. It's actually all too easy though to take a coherent and brilliantly mixed original track, and reduce it to a collection of disparate sounds, and lose the coherence and emotional impact of a piece. So the first thing to make sure of is to "do no harm"! But with care and lots of time, you find a way to present the music in a new way that holds together - and potentially even adds a wonderful extra layer of depth, excitement and emotion."

In addition to the Atmos and 5.1 mixes, the blu-ray also features a Miles Showell 2026 remaster of the original 1976 album made from a new transfer of the original stereo tapes (recently unearthed from Jean-Michel Jarre’s archive). This is unlimited audio presented at the highest possible resolution (192 kHz / 24 bit) – the original version has never sounded better, and possibly never will!

Audio streams on the SDE exclusive Oxygène blu-ray:

• Oxygène – 2026 Dolby Atmos Mix (48 kHz / 24 bit)

• Oxygène – 2026 5.1 Mix (48 kHz / 24 bit)

• Oxygène – 1976 Stereo Mix – Unlimited Miles Showell 2026 Remaster (192 kHz / 24 bit)

• Oxygène – Binaural Mix (headphones only) (48 kHz / 24 bit)

Additionally, the blu-ray includes Oxygène (Part IV) original music video, upgraded to HD, and an exclusive 30 minute video interview with Jean-Michel Jarre, David Kosten and Steven Wilson conducted at Abbey Road Studios earlier this year, during the remastering sessions.

The blu-ray is a hardcover deluxe presentation and comes with 48-page booklet featuring essays from music journalists Alexis Petridis (The Guardian, UK) and Alma Rota (Rolling Stone, France) and David Kosten’s notes about mixing in Dolby Atmos (all three in both French and English). It also includes rare images from the forthcoming book Machines: A History of Electronic Music by Jean-Michel Jarre (to be published by Thames & Hudson on 29 October).

The Oxygene blu-ray containing the Dolby Atmos mix is released on 4 December 2026.

04/Interview

David Kosten

Dolby Atmos Mix

How did you first become involved in music production and specifically what sparked your interest in immersive audio and Dolby Atmos?

After making my own music under the name Faultline, (mostly instrumental music, with occasional guest vocalists including Chris Martin, Michael Stipe and The Flaming Lips) I moved into producing and mixing other artists. I've worked with a really wide range of acts including Keane, Bat For Lashes, Everything Everything, Marina and the Diamonds, Enter Shikari and Steven Wilson.

It was a visit to Dolby HQ with Steven, where we had help mixing his The Future Bites album in Dolby Atmos, that sparked my interest in the format and immersive music in general. I was blown away by the fun sonic possibilities, both for my own music which I'd started to create again, and for the acts I was producing. I was also looking for some new avenues to explore and enjoy, after a long period of really intense work as a producer. Once I'd installed an Atmos speaker rig in my studio, I also started to consider the idea that maybe I could work with classic albums, re-imagining them in an immersive format.

My first commercial job doing this was re-mixing Tubular Bells in Atmos for its 50th anniversary re-issue, and since then I've taken on a few more projects - including Thompson Twins, Heaven 17, Propaganda, Paul Young, Fine Young Cannibals, Keane and Mike Oldfield's second album Hergest Ridge.

Were you aware of Jean Michel Jarre’s music and career ahead of working on Oxygene?

The first record I ever bought was the 7" of Oxygène Part 4. I must have been nine years old. I had a little record player with a built-in speaker, and played the single over and over again. The b-side was Oxygène Part 6 - my favourite track on the album. His music became part of my DNA - every synth sound I make is through that prism and early discovery of Jean-Michel, The Human League, John Foxx, Kraftwerk etc in the late 70's. Nine year old me didn't foresee working with JMJ on Oxygène immersive mixes almost 50 years later of course...

How did the opportunity to create a Dolby Atmos version of Oxygene come about?

Early in 2025 I started sending speculative emails to JMJ's (very patient) manager! I knew the 50th anniversary was coming around, and really wanted to be the person JMJ turned to if this dream project became a reality.

In spring 2026, we started having some serious discussions about getting a demo made, to show how this potentially might sound. And then as soon as JMJ heard the work in progress, it was all systems go...

When dealing with such an iconic album, how do you approach the challenge of respecting the original while bringing something completely new to the listener?

I'm a music fan much more than I am a technician - respecting the source material is vital for my own enjoyment of the end result. And in fact, this was a big reason why I got involved in making Atmos rebuilds of classics - I'd just heard too many average, bland or poor mixes! Either where the new version sounded nothing like the original and hadn't had the love and care needed to bring it back to life accurately, or where the immersive mix was barely a step up from stereo, or a mess, and ruined the original intent of the artist. Or all the above!

I spend hours and hours in the studio fine tuning my work to reflect the original release mix, in as much detail as my ears can detect. The balance between instruments, the tone, use of effects and where the sound sits in the stereo spectrum - I try very hard to bring this all back to life from the raw multitrack data, using my production and mixing experience. This part of the process is a real grind, but if you're lucky enough to be playing with iconic, precious cargo like Oxygène, it's not exactly a hardship!

Often I find that the technical limitations of music originally made primarily for vinyl mean that the lowest (and sometimes highest) frequencies on the master tapes never made it through to the listener, so it's fun to bring those back to life. There's some incredible low bass frequencies on the Oxygène multitracks that have probably never been heard before - with digital there are no limitations regarding low frequency reproduction, so that's often a wonderful and satisfying new thing to capture and reveal. The Atmos format is new too of course - hearing the music completely surround you is an astonishing experience for someone used only to stereo - so even this on its own is a wonderful new prize for a fan of the recording.

I am primarily interested in recreating the original mixes and intentions of the artist, so am not trying to make a 'David' version or 'remix' of it at all - each mix I do of a classic really should sound pretty much like the original - but in a brand new 'exploded three dimensional view'.

What original recordings and source material were available to you, and how did you go about reconstructing the album for an immersive environment? How important was it to preserve the original character and sonic identity of the album?

I was given a digital copy of the original 8 track tape multitrack, from 1976. This had all of JMJ's synth parts and drum machines, in isolation on separate tracks, and also included some of the effects he used too, like the echoes.

This is actually incredibly complex, time consuming and delicate work - many weeks of intense listening to try to recreate the spirit, tone and balance of original mixes, using only raw original multitrack materials, and a final stereo mix as a listening reference to recreate the new mixes from.

I have access to every individual sound and effect used on the tapes to make an album. In essence, I listen to a final stereo mix, and then recreate every nuance of that, using the raw data on the multitrack. I balance the individual sounds, add effects, equalisation and stereo positioning to rebuild an album like Oxygène from scratch, before I move onto the immersive / three dimensional part of the process.

Can you describe some of the creative and technical decisions you made when positioning the sounds around the listener? And the technology you are using?

So this is the really fun part of the process! Once the hard work of recreating the original mixes is done, I start to think about how to present the music in three dimensions. Any sound can be placed anywhere so there's a lot of choices to make across an entire album! With Atmos we have speakers in front, to the side, behind and above the listener. It's actually all too easy though to take a coherent and brilliantly mixed original track, and reduce it to a collection of disparate sounds, and lose the coherence and emotional impact of a piece. So the first thing to make sure of is to "do no harm"! But with care and lots of time, you find a way to present the music in a new way that holds together - and potentially even adds a wonderful extra layer of depth, excitement and emotion.

What was the biggest challenge you encountered, and were there any unexpected discoveries in the original recordings?

There were loads of technical challenges - things are never quite as straightforward as one might hope. I had a few missing sounds or parts that were in need of some sneakery to make work. The birdsong at the end of Part 3 for instance - I had to take that from the original stereo tape as it wasn't on the multitrack. But through that limitation came one of my favourite mix ideas - all the sounds at the end of Part 3 disappearing down the hole of the mono centre speaker - and then the birdsong reappearing overhead.

For a music and synth obsessive like me it's just wonderful hearing the individual elements that go to make up an iconic recording. Often things are much simpler than you realise. Or perhaps a part you've known most of your life is revealed as a combination of two or three different sounds. Also, it's a lot easier to hear the hand-played nature of the synths when you hear them in isolation. Loads of wonderful human timing discrepancies and character are there that kind of dissolve when mixed with other sounds.

How closely was Jean-Michel involved, and what was his reaction when he first heard the finished Atmos mix? Did he give you any specific instructions about how certain sounds or musical passages should be treated?

Neither Steven nor myself have ever had this level of input with a mix from the original artist before. It was just wonderful to have Jean-Michel's ideas and changes, and they made a huge positive impact on the end result. In our Paris sessions together we worked for many hours on detailed changes. How the synths moved in the 3D space, the positioning of the sounds, the tone and balance of the music etc. He was involved in every single second of this mix in one way or another. He would make tons of suggestions about how the sounds should sit together, or work in the immersive space. The idea of having the waves in Part 6 crash from front to back rather than side to side was his for instance. We'd play and keep adjusting detail, fine tuning it until we both were happy. He's an incredibly able listener and instinctive mixer. Do meet your heroes: this one was hilariously funny and kind too. He knew how nervous I must have been, especially in our first session, but he put me at ease and allowed me to work at my best.

There was an enormous amount of work to do before we got to a finished piece. But we shared a satisfied look, and were probably both exhausted at the effort it had taken! We were making changes right up until the final moment before we had to deliver all the files.

Did you ever find yourself having to step back and remind yourself that you were working on an album that millions of people already know and love?

No - it's constantly on my mind - it's a truly daunting responsibility! These are important, iconic pieces of our shared culture. There will be fans who've listened to this record every week for 50 years. They want to know that their beloved music is in safe hands, and I really try to make sure I give them as much respect as the music.

Were there any particular moments where Jean-Michel's reaction surprised you or where he asked you to change something?

After our first few minutes in the studio together I knew what level of attention to detail I was going to get from JMJ, and just how much of a unique experience I was in for. He's a fearless and brave creator, and being in the studio with him was of course an astonishing thrill for me as a fan. I loved every minute, and was kind of sad when we got the album over the line, as I'd enjoyed the project so much!

Having demonstrated the mix to audiences, what has been the most memorable reaction you've witnessed?

It's just enormously satisfying to see people so moved by this work. It can be quite overwhelming to hear your favourite music played in a completely new way - so it's a joy to hear about that afterwards. Once the blu ray and streaming versions come out and everyone can experience it, I hope the reaction remains as positive, and all the work and effort we put into Oxygène simply gives people enormous pleasure!

Do you think immersive audio reveals something about the original recording that simply wasn't possible to appreciate through conventional stereo?

Absolutely. It can and should, otherwise there's not a lot of point in all that effort haha! I guess the experience will be different for every listener, but aside from being able to hear more detail and dynamics, weight and space, the most obvious change would be in the power of the immersive experience. It's thrilling and moving in equal amounts.

If you could take another Jean-Michel Jarre album into Dolby Atmos, which one would it be and why?

Hmmm - isn't Équinoxe going to be 50 quite soon....?!

item.title: If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it
item.description:
Whatever skill you’re learning, it won’t take long before someone with experience in that particular field tells you to get your hands dirty. It’s fine to read “Born to Run”, but you won’t be running an ultra marathon any time soon if you don’t start running. Whether it’s muscle memory, technique, physical fitness or problem solving you need to work on to reach your goals, you need to practice. This isn’t a controversial statement in any field at all, and has never really been.

Except in software engineering, somehow.

When it comes to software engineering, we somehow lost our way, thinking that our skills won’t stop improving if we stop practicing. Making such a claim in any other field would be sneered at at best. Imagine John Scofield1 saying he stopped practicing his guitar because “he was at a good enough level, musically, to maintain (and even improve!) his expertise” simply by 1) instructing others on how to play (either in vibe general terms, or with a strict spec musical notation), and then 2) listening to what they played and iterating until it sounded good enough for his next record. “My music is better”, he would claim, and moreover “actually playing the guitar was never the point anyway, there’s more to making music.”

Mind you, my point in this post is not to discuss the short term quality of code output (or recorded guitar playing, to continue the proverbial thread), but rather the skill of the craftsman practicing his craft vs the one who doesn’t practice at all.

To make another comparison that’s arguably closer to software engineering, or at least the “writing and reasoning about code” part of it, let’s look at authors in other fields. I have no doubt that reading great prose has the potential to nudge a writer towards better writing of his/her own; in fact it’s super important to have creative references to draw upon - no doubt at all. But, imagine an author who 1) stopped writing, and only pursued reading and giving feedback to other writers, and worse yet 2) mostly read AI generated prose!? To be perfectly honest, I would expect a quite steady (if not exponential) decline of this author’s writing skills.

“There’s more to software engineering than writing code” Link to heading

Sure. But if we can at least agree that the code that runs our software is a non-trivial part of it (though, granted, not all of it by far: The other parts of developing and maintaining software speak even louder against using generative AI as a significant tool service!), we should aspire to be proficient in understanding how code works, what good code looks like, what to watch out for and how software architecture plays a vital part in making code Easy To Change.

Simply “reviewing all the code Claude produced” won’t quite cut it. And who are you trying to fool, after all; at this point you’re not really reading half of it, are you?

So I propose something that used to be a no-brainer: Keep practicing!

Which brings me to my next point:

All engineers(!) need to be good at solving problems Link to heading

if || while you can argue that the need for being hands-on on your software’s code varies, I propose you can’t argue that we’re still solving problems. And the moment you stop practicing solving problems is the moment you stop getting better at it, just like everything else. Simple as that. This is hardly new, btw: you could always tell who beat Doom using cheat codes and who finished the game the real way! If the end goal is to “beat the game”, then by all means cheat; if the end goal is getting good at it, then I’d advice you not to. Some lessons are only learned the hard way (trial and error), and very few are learned without effort at all. Repeated LLM usage for problem solving pounds the following premise into our brain’s wiring: If something is hard, tricky or requires effort, you shouldn’t even try. And right there goes our learning, craft and joy, right out the window.

In a world where people are using AI to summarise books instead of reading them and turning to AI for therapy, I don’t want to keep using it. It feels like such a slippery slope. As literacy and numeracy rates decline, I can’t help but question whether encouraging us to rely on AI so heavily is a good idea.

It makes me wonder: are we still thinking for ourselves at all?

— Em’s blog2, emphasis mine.

Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS
item.description:
Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS

Firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world. This is especially true in the EU since 2024, when the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) started requiring Apple to let people choose their default browser; millions have picked Firefox, and daily use on iOS has doubled. People want to choose the browser on their phone.

But there remains an important limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine.

This has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone users because many of these are built within our browser engine, Gecko. iPhones and iPads are unique in having this restriction. On all other major operating systems, including Apple’s macOS, people can access the Gecko-powered version of Firefox.

As a result of the DMA, Apple began allowing alternative browser engines on iOS in the EU. It published a set of conditions that companies like Mozilla must comply with to bring their own browser engine. At the time we said Apple’s rules made it “as painful as possible” for alternatives like Gecko. In the meantime, Japan also introduced new rules requiring alternative browser engines on iOS. Apple applied very similar conditions in Japan to those in the EU.

Nearly three years since Apple introduced these conditions in the EU and almost a year since Japan, not one developer has been able to launch a non-WebKit browser on iOS. The reason is simple: Apple’s conditions remain unworkable. The real test of any rule is whether it delivers the change it was meant to achieve in practice. Compliance on paper alone falls short of that test.

Since the DMA came into effect we’ve been working behind the scenes to test and improve Apple’s conditions so that we can bring Gecko to iOS users. Those efforts have so far largely failed.

One of the conditions requires us not to disclose non-public information related to the project, but here’s an example of what we are up against: to use Gecko, we can’t simply update the Firefox app people already use and love. We’d have to build a whole separate app, a second Firefox. Then we’d have to ask every Firefox user to download it, move their bookmarks, passwords and history across, and manually switch over, step by confusing step.

That’s a lot to ask of people who already made their choice. A significant proportion of people would understandably give up, including many who picked Firefox from the EU’s choice screen.

The conditions Apple imposes, including a level of user friction Apple would never accept for its own apps, mean that the open door feels more like a trap door.

Firefox users on iPhone chose an independent browser. They should get everything that comes with it, including Gecko, the last major browser engine not developed by a big tech company. We’ll keep pushing for a real level playing field, not an opening that drops independent browsers through the floor.

item.title: Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations
item.description:
This repository holds the paper Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations by L. Alpöge and T. Buckmaster and the Lean 4 formalization that accompanies it.

paper/finite-time-blow-up-navier-stokes.pdf: the paper (79 pages, version of 20 November 2026). lean/: the Lean package (Lean v4.33.1 with Mathlib, at the revision pinned in lean/lakefile.toml). lean/README.md explains how the formal statements relate to Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1, Corollary 7.2 and Appendix B of the paper, and where the formal proofs differ from the proofs of the paper.lean/NOTICE says in words what each statement file contains and what is proved.

The statement files at the top of lean/ give the definitions and state the theorems with sorry in place of their proofs; Solution.lean proves them from the library lean/Breakdown/. Each comparator*.json pairs a statement file with Solution.lean, names the theorems whose statements must agree, and permits only the axioms propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice.

To build, from lean/:

lake exe cache get lake build

The library is large (about 2,270 files and 600,000 lines), and a full build needs a great deal of memory and time.

The formalization contains no data. The certificate whose hash the paper gives is not in this repository; the paper says that it will be released. That the certificate satisfies the conditions of Appendix B is verified by a rigorous computation, involving interval arithmetic (128 bits of precision, with the Arb library through FLINT), which is not part of the formalization and is not in this repository either.

The source of the paper is not in this repository.

The package is the one of the paper's working repository, with one patch of 20 November 2026 applied to the cell-layer statements and to the library proofs that depend on them: the weight of one bound becomes $(|m|+\tfrac12)^2$ in place of $m^2+\tfrac14$, one constant of a cell may be zero, and the set of the harmonics of the model in a cell is restricted to those that do not vanish there. Appendix B of the paper states the conditions in this patched form. The patched package was not rebuilt when this repository was assembled.

item.title: I'll never buy Framework hardware again
item.description:
TL;DR:We bought a 3000 EUR Framework Laptop 16 for one of our developers. It was broken out of the box. Three months, around thirty support emails, two replacement parts and a trip to their repair center later, Framework concluded “No Fault Found” and blamed the keyboard layout of an OS that wasn’t even installed when the problem first showed up. I’m done with them. Some context first#

I have been a Framework fan for a while. At my company, developers pick the machine of their choice and several work on Framework laptops or desktops, we have about quite a few of them around, and I have been recommending them to pretty much anyone who asked me what laptop to buy so far. Repairable hardware, Linux-friendly, a company that seemed to care about the people using its products: it was an easy recommendation to make.

So when Q joined the team and needed a workstation, we ordered a Framework Laptop 16, around 3000 EUR once configured.

Three months later, I’m pissed off at Framework and have banned future purchases from them at my company. Not because the machine arrived broken, this happens and I’ve been around hardware long enough to know it, but because of how unprofessional and useless the support has been from the first email to the last.

OH and feel free to share, friends don’t let friends enter hell.

Day one: broken out of the box#

The laptop arrives early August. Q assembles it, powers it on and is greeted by a “missing input module” screen, before reaching the BIOS, before any operating system is even installed. Keep this detail in mind, we’ll get back to it.

The keyboard isn’t detected when centered, and when moved to the left it shows up as… a numpad. In that state, nothing works: not the keyboard, not the touchpad, not the numpad. There’s a BIOS option, “Force Power for Input Modules”, that bypasses module detection. With it enabled, everything works. Without it, the machine has no keyboard and no touchpad. It is recommended NOT to turn it on permanently as it might be harmful to the hardware, as stated on their own website.

I open a ticket on August 13th.

August: the script loop hell#

What follows is two weeks of support reading from a script, one step per email, one email per day or two:

is it out of the box? any damage on the packaging? which OS, which kernel, which BIOS version? do a mainboard reset by pressing the chassis switch ten times reseat the midplate try Force Power On (we had already told them it was the only thing that worked) send photos of the keyboard, the midplate, the connector, the whole laptop from six angles, and a video reset the BIOS to defaults reinstall the BIOS and the drivers bundle (a Windows drivers bundle, for a problem that happens before any OS boots, on a machine that doesn’t run Windows…) try different input module combinations

We did all of it. We sent the photos and the video in a shared drive. Each reply came from a different agent who clearly hadn’t read the thread, and asked for something we had already provided.

On August 24th I lost patience and wrote that this was a 3000 EUR laptop that didn’t work, that my co-worker had been without a usable machine of his own for over a week, and asked them to either send replacement parts or take it back and refund us. I even went all Karen and asked to involve a manager.

Their answer: please send a clear photo of the midplate and the underside of the keyboard. The same photos, again. No manager involved to break the script because no flying fucks were given.

We did their diagnosis for them#

Q then replied from his own address, which apparently is a problem, because support spent the next ten days asking him to “verify the shipping address” of the order, which he did, several times.

Meanwhile, tired of being asked to repeat steps, he updated the keyboard firmware himself (only possible with Force Power On, since the keyboard is otherwise not detected), installed Framework’s own framework_tool, and ran a proper isolation:

$ sudo framework_tool --inputdeck

The result was unambiguous: the keyboard module reports the ID of a numpad, KeyboardB. The firmware therefore sees two numpads and no keyboard, considers the input deck incomplete, and never enables the power rail for the input modules, which is why everything is dead and not just the keyboard.

He moved the keyboard alone across slots: it misidentifies itself in every position. He moved the numpad alone into the same slot: it identifies correctly. He removed everything: the baseline is clean. The wrong ID follows the keyboard. The keyboard is faulty.

He sent all of this to support on August 28th with a full report and a one-line reproduction command.

September: they replace the wrong part#

On September 7th, support concludes… that the midplate needs to be replaced. Not the keyboard, the only part that a reproducible diagnostic, run with their own tool, had just pointed at.

The midplate arrives a week later. The problem is, of course, still there because… GOTO previous paragraph. Q asks them whether they’re sure it’s not the keyboard, given that he proved it with the diagnosis.

Their answer ?

Back to the queue. Back to photos: the packaging box from different angles including the interior, the midplate front and back, the keyboard top and bottom, close-ups of the sockets. Photos they already had.

At this point, Q is no longer a developer but has become a profesionnal photographer.

October: a new keyboard, a new bug#

On October 8th, two months after the laptop arrived, Framework finally agrees to replace the keyboard. What they should have done on the first week…

The new keyboard is detected, the original bug is gone, but there is a new one: pressing C sends a c followed by a Delete escape sequence.

$ showkey -a c 99 0143 0x63 ^[[3~ 27 0033 0x1b 91 0133 0x5b 51 0063 0x33 126 0176 0x7e

An external keyboard on the same machine produces a single c, as it should.

FU-CKIN’ HELL it never ends…

You can’t use a keyboard where typing a word containing a c deletes the next character. You certainly can’t type a disk encryption passphrase with it.

Q is smart so he knows the drill and sends the showkey output, photos, and a video to avoid wasting time on a useless round-trip, but he understimated them: support asks him whether the issue happens with an external keyboard (he had already said it didn’t), then asks him to boot a live USB to “isolate software issues” (yes, the famous ones that would trigger on just their keyboard). He does, tries both the US and French layouts, same result as anyone not brain-dead would expect.

The ticket is escalated, with the usual “escalations may take 5 to 7 working days”.

November: “No Fault Found”#

End of October, Framework decides to have the laptop sent to their repair center for a “full review and assessment”, with a reminder that we may be charged if they find customer-induced damage.

We ship it.

This morning, November 20th, the verdict arrives:

Our repair center has completed their diagnostics, tested two keyboards and found that they were working perfectly. They have determined No Fault Found and that the issue was likely caused by installing the wrong keyboard layout in the operating system.

Let me be very clear about why this is nonsense:

Keyboard 1 failed before any operating system was installed on the machine. The “missing input module” screen shows up before the BIOS. There was no keyboard layout to get wrong. However, the BIOS workaround they asked us to enable was still on when the laptop was shipped, and with it on, the problem is hidden. If you don’t turn it off, you won’t see the fault. Keyboard 2 fails in GRUB, before the kernel is even loaded, and on a live USB with both QWERTY and AZERTY layouts, which, by the way, put the C key in the same place. A keyboard layout maps a key to a character; it does not make a key emit two scancodes. And if you test by typing a sentence and looking at the result, a spurious Delete at the end of a line deletes nothing and you’ll never notice it. You have to actually look at what the key sends, which is exactly what we showed them.

So either the repair center tested with the workaround on and never pressed C in the middle of a word, or they didn’t test at all. In both cases, “the user picked the wrong keyboard layout” is not a diagnosis, it’s a way to close a ticket.

What it cost us#

Let’s count:

three months and one week since the laptop arrived, around thirty emails from support, handled by more than a dozen different agents, two replacement parts, one of which was the wrong one, a round trip to a repair center, hours of an engineer’s time spent producing photos, videos, reports and diagnostics that the support team then didn’t read, a developer who had to work for weeks with external devices plugged into a laptop that couldn’t be used as a laptop.

And at the end, the laptop comes back in the exact state it left, with a note implying we don’t know how to configure a keyboard layout.

The problem isn’t the hardware#

Hardware fails. A bad keyboard module out of the box is annoying, not scandalous. I’ve had DOA hardware from every vendor I’ve ever bought from.

What’s scandalous is the process:

nobody owns the ticket, every reply comes from someone new who restarts from a script; information we provide is not read, so it gets requested again, and again; a clear, reproducible diagnosis made with their own tool is ignored in favor of replacing an unrelated part; basic customer identity handling is broken enough that a colleague replying on the thread triggers ten days of address verification; and when it finally reaches people who could actually look at the hardware, the conclusion contradicts facts that were in the ticket from day one.

What’s scandalous is the amount of not giving a damn, not escalating, not caring at all about having a customer in a shit situation for more than three months when they could simply replace the broken part and be done. Like they can’t afford a spare keyboard and make sure that it works ?

So, what now?#

We’re not going to spend another three months trying to get Framework to acknowledge a fault we’ve demonstrated a dozen times when they obviously don’t care. We’ll recycle the laptop into a desktop when it comes back from the repair center and will get Q a new laptop from another vendor that’s more serious and professional.

As for me: buying new Framework hardware is now off the table. The machines we have will live their lives, but the next ones will come from somewhere else.

I liked the idea of Framework a lot. Repairability is worthless if the company behind it can’t tell a broken keyboard from a keyboard layout nor… repair, and the support I’ve experienced is the opposite of what I’d expect from a company selling premium-priced hardware to professionals.

If you’re considering a Framework for your company, I hope it works out of the box for you. Because if it doesn’t, you now know what’s waiting for you.

item.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
item.description:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

[Submitted on 16 Nov 2026 (v1), last revised 18 Nov 2026 (this version, v2)]

Title:Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own WeightsView PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract:A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training. PostgreSQL 19: A hands-on tour with runnable browser examples
item.description:
PostgreSQL 19: less friction, more control

Run the new SQL, inspect the planner, and replicate between real PostgreSQL 19 servers.

A release you can try at the prompt

PostgreSQL 19 brings useful new SQL alongside maintenance and replication improvements. Try IGNORE NULLS, get-or-create inserts, JSON export, JSONPath transformations, and range subtraction, then explore planner advice and real replication.

PostgreSQL 19.0 · released 19 November 2026. The stable release announcement introduces the version installed in this sandbox. Each feature links to its official documentation. The release notes remain the complete change log.

About this terminal. Experiments run on a real PostgreSQL 19 server as student, in a disposable guest. Maintenance tables live in blog_lab. Replication experiments start additional real servers on demand: a logical subscriber on 5433, and a physical standby on 5434, both fed by the primary on 5432. To fit the guest’s memory budget, only one of these extra instances runs at a time: each replication card stops the other and starts its own. Re-run that card before checking its current state again. Their first runs take longer because they initialize a cluster or take a base backup. Reset discards all three clusters and their data.

How to compare with 18. Sidenotes offer older SQL/workflows that you can run on 19, or a setting that disables a particular new optimization. These show the difference in expression or behavior. They do not turn PostgreSQL 19 into PostgreSQL 18. For timing claims, run the same workload on actual 18 and 19 servers with equal data, settings, cache conditions, and hardware.

Run the experiments in any order. Commands beginning with \! run a shell command from psql. The logical replication walkthrough shows its server setup and SQL directly; as-postgres runs server utilities as the Linux postgres account. Query and comparison examples state when to use another port or the administrative SQL role.

Start with the server you actually have

Before reading a release article, ask the server which release you are actually running. SELECT 1 is also a pleasantly boring connectivity test: a result beats a spinning status indicator.

The version returned below belongs to the sandbox, not to the release covered by the article. The SQL role is student; ownership of the prepared demo database gives you room to experiment without administrative credentials.

Look for: one row, a real server version, and the expected role. Keep that baseline when you compare an upgrade later.

From the shell, open the demo database (PGDATABASE=blog_lab):

psql

Then run this at the SQL prompt:

SELECT 1 AS terminal_is_alive, current_setting('server_version') AS actual_version, current_user AS sql_role;

Expected: One row with terminal_is_alive = 1, the installed server version, and student.

REPACK — rewrite and reclaim space

Deleting rows leaves reusable space behind. Regular vacuum cleans that space; PostgreSQL 19’s native REPACK rewrites the table and returns unused bytes to the OS. The card deletes middle rows, preserving occupied tail pages so ordinary vacuum cannot simply truncate them. Compare the file size after vacuum with its size after a real rewrite. The tiny table demonstrates the operation, not a storage benchmark. REPACK documentation.

The concurrent variant uses logical decoding to capture intervening writes and takes an access-exclusive lock for the final swap. After the card, run this example at the same psql prompt. REPACK requires the table's MAINTAIN privilege; student owns events, so no role change is needed.

REPACK (CONCURRENTLY, ANALYZE) events;

Compare with 18: VACUUM (FULL, ANALYZE) events; performs the older blocking rewrite. For physical index ordering, compare CLUSTER events USING events_pkey; with REPACK events USING INDEX events_pkey;. Restore the same bloated table before each run. Use a second connection to try SELECT/INSERT while a larger rewrite runs, and inspect pg_locks: the concurrent form still locks briefly at the swap. PostgreSQL 18 has no native concurrent equivalent; the separately installed pg_repack extension is another workflow.

 DELETE FROM events WHERE id BETWEEN 301 AND 700; VACUUM (ANALYZE) events; SELECT pg_relation_size('events') AS bytes_before_repack; REPACK (ANALYZE) events; SELECT count(*) AS surviving_events, pg_relation_size('events') AS bytes_after_repack FROM events WHERE id <= 1000;

Expected: DELETE 400 on the first run, VACUUM, REPACK, then 600 original surviving events. Compare bytes before/after; sizes vary.

Autovacuum — inspect the real priority scores

Autovacuum now prioritizes tables using real scores and can parallelize index work. The card reads pg_stat_autovacuum_scores and the configured score weights. Use \x on to show the wide scores view as readable records, then \x off to return to a table for the two-column settings query. Scores change with workload and statistics, so zero after maintenance is a useful result too. Autovacuum scheduling, statistics views.

autovacuum_max_parallel_workers controls the server-wide allowance; autovacuum_parallel_workers is a per-table setting. The sandbox’s current parallel allowance is zero, so the card inspects priorities rather than launching parallel vacuum work. PostgreSQL 19 can also mark eligible pages all-visible during ordinary scans, improving future index-only scans.

Compare with 18: On an administrative connection, set autovacuum_max_parallel_workers = 0 with ALTER SYSTEM, then reload using SELECT pg_reload_conf(); to disable this new parallel index work. Restore the previous value afterward. Manual VACUUM (PARALLEL 0) versus VACUUM (PARALLEL 2) is also runnable on 18, but measures manual vacuum. There is no faithful switch back to PostgreSQL 18’s autovacuum scheduler; compare the scheduling on separate installations.

 \x on SELECT * FROM pg_stat_autovacuum_scores WHERE relid IN ('events'::regclass, 'orders'::regclass); \x off SELECT name, setting FROM pg_settings WHERE name LIKE 'autovacuum%score_weight' OR name = 'autovacuum_max_parallel_workers' ORDER BY name;

Expected: Expanded records for per-table scores, then a two-column table of configured weights; recently vacuumed tables may score zero.

Plan advice — constrain one query, then release it

pg_plan_advice generates a description of planner choices and lets you constrain selected choices. pg_stash_advice stores advice by query identifier for automatic reuse. In this database setup has enabled the advice module for the student’s sessions; on another installation an administrator can use LOAD 'pg_plan_advice' or configure preloading. Plan advice, stored advice.

The first plan emits generated advice; the second requests SEQ_SCAN(orders). Look for matched feedback. Advice restricts the normal planner and can become stale when data changes.

Compare with 18: Run the settings, query, and resets in the same connection:

 SET enable_indexscan = off; SET enable_bitmapscan = off; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT sum(amount) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1; RESET enable_indexscan; RESET enable_bitmapscan;

These broad settings discourage whole classes of paths. PostgreSQL 19’s advice can instead target a named table in a query. Our small table is likely to choose a sequential scan already; the interesting evidence is the advice and its feedback.

Inspect the generated plan advice.

EXPLAIN (PLAN_ADVICE, COSTS OFF) SELECT sum(amount) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1;

Apply session advice, inspect the plan, then reset the setting.

SET pg_plan_advice.advice = 'SEQ_SCAN(orders)'; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS OFF) SELECT sum(amount) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1; RESET pg_plan_advice.advice;

Expected: Generated Plan Advice, then Supplied Plan Advice with matched feedback and an Aggregate plan.

Logical replication — see what moves between two servers

Follow one row and one counter from source to destination. The publisher on 5432 owns the source data. The subscriber on 5433 is a separate PostgreSQL process with its own data directory. Both databases are named pg19_repl; the port identifies which one you are changing.

Object Publisher · 5432 Subscriber · 5433 messages Write a row The publication copies the row scratch Write a row Excluded from the publication; remains empty ticket_numbers Consume 50 values Explicit refresh copies the sequence state

The commands below show the entire setup. Run them in order, or use Run all steps to enter the same visible commands. \! runs a shell command from psql. as-postgres runs the following command as the Linux postgres account; initdb initializes the cluster and pg_ctl starts it. \connect database role host port chooses the SQL connection. Administrative SQL here explicitly uses the SQL role postgres. Local trust authentication is for this disposable guest.

The standby from experiment 06 is stopped first to fit the guest's memory budget. The subscriber uses small buffers and synchronous I/O for this runtime. Its log is /tmp/pg19-subscriber.log. Conditional setup preserves existing objects on repeat runs; each repeat advances the publisher counter again.

What is new in 19? FOR ALL TABLES EXCEPT (TABLE scratch) excludes a table, and ALL SEQUENCES includes sequence state. Initial subscription creation copies sequence values; later publisher calls to nextval can leave the subscriber behind. REFRESH SEQUENCES requests another copy. We wait for the initial copy before advancing the publisher so it cannot mask the before/after comparison. The visible polling loops have a deadline because synchronization is asynchronous. Definitions must match on both servers. Sequence synchronization, publication syntax.

The subscription receives data over loopback TCP; psql uses local Unix sockets for administration. Compare wal_level = replica with effective_wal_level = logical on the publisher after creating the publication: PostgreSQL 19 enables logical WAL when required without restarting this primary. WAL configuration.

Compare with 18: Publish the included table explicitly with FOR TABLE messages. The publisher needs wal_level = logical and a restart. Sequence state is not replicated: at cutover, stop publisher writes, read last_value and is_called, and apply setval('ticket_numbers', captured_value, captured_is_called) on the subscriber. In 19, repeat the steps below and compare the counter before and after REFRESH SEQUENCES.

1 · Make room for the subscriber. Stop the physical standby only if experiment 06 has started it.

\! if as-postgres pg_ctl status -D /tmp/pg19-standby >/dev/null 2>&1; then as-postgres pg_ctl stop -D /tmp/pg19-standby -m fast -w; fi

2 · Initialize a separate cluster. initdb creates its data directory; the condition preserves it on repeat runs.

\! if ! as-postgres test -f /tmp/pg19-subscriber/PG_VERSION; then as-postgres initdb -D /tmp/pg19-subscriber -U postgres --auth=trust --locale=C -E UTF8; fi

3 · Start that cluster on port 5433. pg_ctl waits for startup; the -o options choose the port, sockets, and small memory settings for this guest.

\! as-postgres pg_ctl status -D /tmp/pg19-subscriber || as-postgres pg_ctl start -D /tmp/pg19-subscriber -l /tmp/pg19-subscriber.log -w -o "-p 5433 -h 127.0.0.1 -k /tmp -c dynamic_shared_memory_type=mmap -c shared_buffers=16MB -c max_connections=10 -c io_method=sync"

4 · Publisher, port 5432. Create the source database if absent. psql’s \gexec executes the CREATE DATABASE text only when the SELECT returns it.

\connect postgres postgres /tmp 5432 SELECT 'CREATE DATABASE pg19_repl OWNER student' WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT FROM pg_database WHERE datname = 'pg19_repl') \gexec

5 · Publisher schema and publication. messages is included, scratch is excluded, and ticket_numbers is explicitly published through ALL SEQUENCES. The existence checks make setup repeatable.

\connect pg19_repl postgres /tmp 5432 CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS messages (id integer PRIMARY KEY, body text); CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS scratch (id integer); CREATE SEQUENCE IF NOT EXISTS ticket_numbers START 1; SELECT 'CREATE PUBLICATION pg19_pub FOR ALL TABLES EXCEPT (TABLE scratch), ALL SEQUENCES' WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT FROM pg_publication WHERE pubname = 'pg19_pub') \gexec SELECT pubname, puballtables, puballsequences FROM pg_publication; SHOW wal_level; SHOW effective_wal_level;

6 · Subscriber, port 5433. Create the destination database and matching objects. Logical replication does not create their definitions.

\connect postgres postgres /tmp 5433 SELECT 'CREATE DATABASE pg19_repl' WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT FROM pg_database WHERE datname = 'pg19_repl') \gexec \connect pg19_repl postgres /tmp 5433 CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS messages (id integer PRIMARY KEY, body text); CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS scratch (id integer); CREATE SEQUENCE IF NOT EXISTS ticket_numbers START 1;

7 · Subscriber. Subscribe to the publisher on 5432. The connection string is the source; the current psql connection is the destination.

SELECT $sql$CREATE SUBSCRIPTION pg19_sub CONNECTION 'host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 user=postgres dbname=pg19_repl' PUBLICATION pg19_pub$sql$ WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT FROM pg_subscription WHERE subname = 'pg19_sub') \gexec

8 · Wait for the initial sequence copy before changing the publisher. This visible shell loop checks synchronization metadata, with up to 300 checks, sleeping 0.1 seconds between checks.

\! ready=0; for attempt in $(seq 1 300); do if [ "$(psql -w -X -h /tmp -p 5433 -U postgres -d pg19_repl -At -c "SELECT count(*) FROM pg_subscription_rel WHERE srrelid = 'ticket_numbers'::regclass AND srsublsn IS NOT NULL")" = 1 ]; then ready=1; break; fi; sleep 0.1; done; test "$ready" = 1 && echo 'Initial sequence copy ready' || echo 'Initial sequence copy timed out' >&2

9 · Publisher. Write one included row and one excluded row. Advance the sequence 50 times so the change crosses a sequence WAL batch; record publisher_ticket.

\connect pg19_repl postgres /tmp 5432 INSERT INTO messages VALUES (1, 'hello from the publisher') ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET body = EXCLUDED.body; INSERT INTO scratch SELECT 1 WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT FROM scratch WHERE id = 1); SELECT max(n) AS publisher_ticket FROM (SELECT nextval('ticket_numbers') AS n FROM generate_series(1, 50)) q; SELECT last_value AS publisher_ticket, is_called FROM ticket_numbers;

10 · Subscriber, before refresh. Its counter can lag even while table changes replicate. Compare subscriber_ticket with the publisher value above.

\connect pg19_repl postgres /tmp 5433 SELECT last_value AS subscriber_ticket_before_refresh, is_called FROM ticket_numbers;

11 · Subscriber. Request sequence synchronization explicitly. ALTER SUBSCRIPTION schedules asynchronous work; it does not wait for the new value.

ALTER SUBSCRIPTION pg19_sub REFRESH SEQUENCES;

12 · Wait for equal sequence values and the included row. The SQL and deadline are visible here; this loop only observes the servers.

\! target=$(psql -w -X -h /tmp -p 5432 -U postgres -d pg19_repl -At -c 'SELECT last_value FROM ticket_numbers'); synced=0; for attempt in $(seq 1 300); do if [ "$(psql -w -X -h /tmp -p 5433 -U postgres -d pg19_repl -At -c "SELECT (last_value = $target AND is_called AND EXISTS (SELECT FROM messages WHERE id = 1 AND body = 'hello from the publisher'))::int FROM ticket_numbers")" = 1 ]; then synced=1; break; fi; sleep 0.1; done; test "$synced" = 1 && echo 'Sequence synchronization confirmed' || echo 'Sequence synchronization timed out' >&2

13 · Subscriber evidence. messages contains the published row, scratch stays empty, and subscriber_ticket matches publisher_ticket. Inspect the synchronization metadata, then return to blog_lab as student.

SELECT * FROM messages; SELECT count(*) AS excluded_scratch_rows FROM scratch; SELECT last_value AS subscriber_ticket_after_refresh, is_called FROM ticket_numbers; SELECT srrelid::regclass, srsubstate, srsublsn FROM pg_subscription_rel ORDER BY 1; \connect blog_lab student /tmp 5432

Expected: messages contains 1 | hello from the publisher; excluded_scratch_rows is 0; subscriber_ticket_after_refresh matches publisher_ticket. Configured WAL is replica; effective WAL is logical. A timeout means synchronization has not been confirmed. Values advance on repeat runs.

WAIT — trace a committed write to a physical standby

A write can commit on the primary before a standby can read it. This walkthrough follows an event with ID 2000 from the primary on 5432 to a physical standby on 5434. Unlike the logical subscriber in section 05, a physical standby starts from a backup of the entire cluster and replays WAL to keep that copy current.

Run the steps in order, or use Run all steps. Every server command and SQL statement is shown below. \! executes a shell command from psql; as-postgres runs server utilities as the Linux postgres account. SQL writes and reads use student, and each \connect identifies the destination port. The logical subscriber is stopped first to fit the guest’s memory budget. The backup and its replication slot are reused on repeat runs. Physical standby setup.

The read follows three stages: commit the write → capture its WAL position → wait for standby replay. Capture the LSN after the INSERT has committed. Waiting for WAL to arrive or be flushed does not establish that the rows have been applied. MODE 'standby_replay' waits for that application step; the following SELECT obtains a fresh snapshot. Keep WAIT outside an explicit transaction for this example. WAIT documentation.

Look for: success from WAIT, then is_standby = true, replay_reached_target = true, and the expected row. If WAIT times out, inspect /tmp/pg19-standby.log and retry the wait after resolving the delay. Do not treat a timeout as permission to perform the dependent read. If a failover changes the timeline, establish whether the captured LSN still refers to the expected history.

Compare with 18: Poll SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= :'target_lsn'::pg_lsn; on the standby with a short sleep and an overall deadline. Read only after it returns true. PostgreSQL 19’s WAIT performs that wait inside the server. Optional NO_THROW returns timeout or not in recovery as a status instead of an error; your application must handle that status before reading.

1 · Make room for the physical standby. Connect to the primary before stopping the logical subscriber from experiment 05; only one extra server fits in this guest.

\connect blog_lab student /tmp 5432 \! if as-postgres pg_ctl status -D /tmp/pg19-subscriber >/dev/null 2>&1; then as-postgres pg_ctl stop -D /tmp/pg19-subscriber -m fast -w; fi

2 · Copy the primary cluster. pg_basebackup takes the initial physical backup from port 5432. -R configures standby mode and its upstream connection; -X stream includes WAL generated during the backup. -C -S creates a named replication slot that retains WAL for this standby. The condition reuses the backup on repeat runs.

\! if ! as-postgres test -f /tmp/pg19-standby/PG_VERSION; then as-postgres pg_basebackup -h /tmp -p 5432 -U postgres -D /tmp/pg19-standby -R -X stream -c fast -C -S pg19_standby; fi

3 · Give the copied cluster its own port. It inherits the primary’s configuration, so override port 5432 with 5434. Empty preloaded libraries and disabled log collection keep this extra instance within the guest’s memory budget.

\! as-postgres sh -c "printf '%s\n' 'port = 5434' \"shared_preload_libraries = ''\" 'logging_collector = off' >> /tmp/pg19-standby/postgresql.auto.conf"

4 · Start the standby. pg_ctl starts PostgreSQL from the copied data directory and waits until it accepts connections. A running standby is left running; startup messages go to /tmp/pg19-standby.log.

\! as-postgres pg_ctl status -D /tmp/pg19-standby || as-postgres pg_ctl start -D /tmp/pg19-standby -l /tmp/pg19-standby.log -w

5 · Verify the destination. Connect to blog_lab on 5434 as student. is_standby must be true and port must be 5434. A physical backup includes the database and its tables; no CREATE TABLE is needed here.

\connect blog_lab student /tmp 5434 SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() AS is_standby, current_setting('port') AS port;

6 · Commit a write on the primary. Switch to 5432, enable psql autocommit, and insert an event with ID 2000. The next command runs after this INSERT commits. ON CONFLICT makes the demonstration repeatable.

\connect blog_lab student /tmp 5432 \set AUTOCOMMIT on INSERT INTO events VALUES (2000, 'replica-visible write') ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET payload = EXCLUDED.payload;

7 · Capture the WAL position after commit. An LSN is a position in the write-ahead log. This position is at or beyond our transaction’s commit record. psql’s \gset saves it as target_lsn; \echo shows the value. The client variable survives switching servers.

SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn() AS target_lsn \gset \echo Target WAL position: :target_lsn

8 · Wait on the standby for replay. Switch to 5434 and substitute the saved LSN with :'target_lsn'. standby_replay waits until WAL has been applied to the database. TIMEOUT limits the wait to 30 seconds; an error stops Run all steps before the read. A caught-up standby returns success immediately.

\connect blog_lab student /tmp 5434 WAIT FOR LSN :'target_lsn' WITH (MODE 'standby_replay', TIMEOUT '30s');

9 · Read after WAIT succeeds. This separate SELECT takes a fresh snapshot on the standby. Expect is_standby and replay_reached_target to be true, plus the event with ID 2000 and payload replica-visible write. Finally return to the primary for the next experiment.

SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() AS is_standby, pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= :'target_lsn'::pg_lsn AS replay_reached_target, id, payload FROM events WHERE id = 2000; \connect blog_lab student /tmp 5432

Expected: On port 5434: is_standby = true; WAIT returns success; the separate read shows replay_reached_target = true and the event with ID 2000 and payload replica-visible write. Target LSN values vary. A timeout means the standby has not replayed the target yet.

Foreign keys — faster inserts, same contract

Most application schemas have relationships. Here, a customer can have zero or many orders, and each order can reference zero or one customer because customer_id is nullable. Every non-NULL customer reference must exist, so foreign-key checking is on the hot path for an ordinary order insert.

The Beta 1 announcement reported up to roughly twice the insert performance for workloads involving foreign-key checks. That is a workload-specific result, not a promise that every INSERT becomes twice as fast.

Insert a demo order, then join it to the customer. The ON CONFLICT clause makes the experiment repeatable. An insert referencing a nonexistent customer would still be rejected: faster checking preserves the constraint's job.

Look for: order 1001 attached to Ada. To evaluate the upgrade, replay realistic batches with the same relationships, transaction sizes, and contention. Do not turn off constraints to make the comparison look better.

INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1001, 1, 42) ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING; SELECT o.id, c.name, o.amount FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.id = 1001;

Expected: INSERT 0 1 on the first run, then 1001 | Ada | 42.

IGNORE NULLS — carry the last known value forward

lag, lead, first_value, last_value, and nth_value now support IGNORE NULLS. Here, last_value carries the most recent known reading through gaps. The explicit frame ends at the current row so no future observation leaks backward. Window functions.

Compare with 18: A running maximum is wrong when readings decrease. Run this older two-window workaround on the same data and compare its result with the card:

 -- PostgreSQL 18 approach: group readings, then fill each group. WITH islands AS ( SELECT tick, reading, count(reading) OVER (ORDER BY tick ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS grp FROM readings ) SELECT tick, reading, max(reading) OVER (PARTITION BY grp) AS carried FROM islands ORDER BY tick;

Each non-null value starts a new group. The results match; the 19 expression needs one window rather than the grouping workaround.

-- PostgreSQL 19 approach: carry the latest non-null reading forward. SELECT tick, reading, last_value(reading) IGNORE NULLS OVER ( ORDER BY tick ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW ) AS carried FROM readings ORDER BY tick;

Expected: Carried values 10, 10, 7, 7, while the original missing readings remain NULL.

Get or create — return the conflict without updating it

ON CONFLICT DO SELECT ... RETURNING implements get-or-create without a dummy update. Run it twice: the second call returns the existing ID and tuple xmin. Optional FOR UPDATE / FOR SHARE can lock the conflicting row. INSERT documentation.

Compare with 18: Replace DO SELECT with DO UPDATE SET handle = EXCLUDED.handle and repeat. It returns the ID, but also creates a new row version and can fire UPDATE triggers. Inspect xmin before/after; under autocommit it changes. DO NOTHING RETURNING returns no row on conflict. The common single-statement CTE fallback can miss a concurrently inserted row under READ COMMITTED; an insert-then-select retry loop is another 18 approach. Sequence gaps can occur even on the new conflict path because defaults are evaluated before resolving the conflict.

 INSERT INTO handles(handle) VALUES ('ada') ON CONFLICT (handle) DO SELECT RETURNING id, handle, xmin;

Expected: Both calls return the same id and xmin for ada; the second call selects the existing row.

range_minus_multi returns each non-empty remaining range as a row. multirange_minus_multi returns a non-empty multirange result, or no rows if nothing remains. Useful for availability minus booked time. Range functions.
